doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Will Bradley's offer, Nola Studios and sneaking into Chico's rehearsal
summary: Will Bradley invited Astor's band to join him; Marty waited for the Maxted chair, haunted Nola Studios and walked in on Chico Marx's band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: How about when you were first married and you were on the road? What kind of salary were you getting?

Well that’s a long story. You see when I left Bob Astor’s band, before I left Bob Astor’s band we were working in Youngstown, Ohio at the Elms Ballroom. And we were there for four weeks. And there was a local theater where bands used to come in and play, and what’s his name, Ray McKinley and Wilbur, the trombone player, now the age is catching me. Ray McKinley and Will Bradley, Bradley-McKinley, you know, 18th and Chestnut, between 18th and 19th on whatever, you know. Anyway, they came into town. They were thinking of splitting up. So I told Will Bradley, Will Bradley came to the Elms Ballroom and he heard us play and he flipped out. And he took some of us on the side on one of the breaks and he said, “you know Ray McKinley and I are breaking up,” and he says, “you guys are great, and I’m starting a new band and I’d love to have you guys with me.” And we said, “yeah,” because we were like young kids, it was the first band. You get an offer from a guy like Will Bradley, you say “I’m ready, I’m ready.” So what happened, we went back to New York, the band had some time off, we went back to New York and I went to the rehearsal. And now the piano player with Will Bradley’s band was a fellow named Billy Maxted. He wrote all the arrangements. In fact he wrote the arrangements with Chico Marx’s band see? So he wrote the arrangements for Bradley’s

band, and when Bradley wanted us to join his band, most of the guys with Astor’s band went with him, including me, but the thing was that Billy Maxted, when I went to the rehearsal he was playing piano and he says, “I’m not leaving the band until I get my money, because he owes me a lot of money for arrangements, see, and when I get my money I’ll call you, and you take my place.” I says okay. So in the meantime I used to go to Local 802. First we’d go to Local 802 to look for jobs, and then we would go to Nola Studios, where all the musicians used to hang out. And Nola Studios, did you ever hear of that name? Nola Studios? It was on Broadway and 52nd Street, 51st Street, upstairs where now there’s a hair, they teach girls how to make hair, whatever. And this place was huge. It was the whole floor, from 51st to 52nd Street, they had about twelve different studios, rehearsal studios. Every band that came into town rehearsed at Nola Studios. Bands would come into town— And every room had a door with a mail slot in it. So we would go up there if somebody was rehearsing, we’d look in the mail slot to see who was rehearsing, and try and sneak in and listen to the band. So I came up there one day and there was a girl receptionist, Ella Jean, and I said, “hey Ella Jean, who’s rehearsing today?” So I heard this music as I got out of the elevator, a big band coming from that room. And I said, “who’s in that room, the band sounds great.” She said, “Chico Marx.” I said, “the Marx Brothers?” She said, “no not the Marx brothers, just Chico, the piano player.” I said, “oh that’s great.” So I went over to the door to peek in the door to see what I could see. And as I went to open the slot, the door opened and somebody walked out and I snuck in. So I closed the door quietly and as I’m standing there, somebody in the band says, “hey Benny, there he is now.” And the whole band is looking at me. And there’s nobody in the room but the orchestra and me. So I gave it the old classic, “who, me?” So this guy comes over to me and he says, “hey, are you Marty Napoleon?” I said, “yeah, how did you know that?” He said, “we called your house, your wife said you went to the union.” I said, “yeah I was at the union and I just came over here to see who was rehearsing.” I said, “who are you?” He says, “I’m Ben Pollack, I’m the manager of the Chico Marx band.” He says, “would you like to try out for the band?” I says, “what?” Because see he called Maxted, because the piano player gave his notice. Benny called Billy Maxted. Maxted said, “call this kid” because he had my number. He said, “call him” so he called my house and my wife said, “he went to the union.”
